text: I have not played it in this free weekend, but considering that it being free right now enables me to finally make a review from my playtime in the beta, I will do so. The game is bad. I am sorry. There is a reason this game has a low player number, and sure, partly it is because of the bad release timing, but the game itself is NOT what I want in an arena shooter. The enviroments are too flashy, the characters have absolutely zero personality or are in any way likeable. The game tries to be edgy and cool around every single corner and it is irritating to no end. Balance is nonexistent; the game has classes, but some are useless while some are way too present and ruin every game. While the game captures the fast-paced feel of old arena shooters like Quake or UT very well when just moving around, it certainly does not capture the gameplay. EVERY GAMEMODE but one revolves around capturing or holding objectives. Wanna have fun standing in a circle for 15 seconds in a fast-paced game? Imagine doing that in Quake. Fun? Not in the slightest. While Quake had modes like this, they were still faster and worked better; and still deathmach was more popular. The game launched without a deathmatch mode as well which, in my opinion, would've been the only fun thing to do in the game, and the lack of a deathmatch mode at launch certainly contributed to the rapid death. The only good modes in this game are the new skirmish kinda mode because it is the closest thing to deathmatch, and blitzball because you actually get to use the movement options in the game. Turf Wars sucks (holding three objectives at a time because ???), and the Battery/Uplink modes, which are both essentially the same modes but with different names(?), suck as well. Long story short, the game's biggest problems are the lack of balance between classes, the uninspired and for an fast paced arena shooter (largely) thematically stupid objectives, and the extremely boring aesthetic. Everything looks the same, future-y I guess, but still extremely boring. The graphics are great thanks to the engine, but that does not save the boring aesthetic. I had fun playing it in the free weekend on my first day, but on the second I began realizing the many glaring flaws and problems. It is a shame, too - with some rebalancing, a new vision and a different aesthetic, this could have been THE new modern day quake, just with classes. Sadly, they ruined it and the lead developers rude comments towards skeptics don't help. I would say definitely skip this one until it becomes fully free to play. Then, it won't hurt checking it out, but for now, stay away - this does not emulate the old glory days of arena shooters, it is a boring, uninspired and unbalanced mess.

title: LiEat
text: Short and sweet is what I would describe this. LiEat is a story about a small dragon that eats lies and a man that lies. The story is divided into 3 acts, each involving its own mystery. Its not much of a game. Its incredibly easy, not too challenging, even when there is a little bit of gameplay. Luckily its a story driven experience. It was a little confusing to tell what I needed to do next, and it required a little of trial and error. You needed to do some things in order so I ended up doing same things over and over until I got it all in order. The game is short, which I think is a good thing. I liked the characters. I found all of them to be interesting and fun. The story was good, but I also wish there was more of it. Its a complex thing, because I think the game has a good length and it ends well, but I also was left feeling that we're not quite done with these characters. I should also add that the short animations were fantastic, whenever there was animation. I wish there was an anime with that style made out of this, but I somehow doubt that will happen. Overall, it is an enjoyable game that manages to tell a sweet, endearing story in short amount of time, but the gameplay holds it back. If you want a story that's sweet like candy, then I recommend this to you.

title: LiEat
text: LiEat: ~~~~ I guess everybody in their lifetime has managed to tell a couple of lies (or embellish the truth) here and there. Well, imagine you come across “Leo,” a caretaker, and “Efina,” a demon who is a lie detector, nourishing herself by eating lies. You would probably be in a rather awkward position, wouldn’t you say? LiEat is a rich story /JRPG game where you play “Efina” and her caretaker in three very well written short stories (LiEat I, II and III). Leo is essentially a con artist who is selling information from one town to the next and keeps changing his name and appearance all the time. Efina was born from a dragon egg; she has the appearance a four year-old child but she is only two months old. She call Leo (Hal, Theo, Albert and god knows what) “Papa” (father) due to the fact that he has raised her since she hatched. In each location they visit, they will be faced with strange events, will investigate them and aim to find all the culprits. You will interact with interesting characters in each of the stories and even have the ability to read their bio’s at the end of each episode. I like that, as it really reinforces the thoughts behind all the characters in their journey. There is a combat phase, which is not the big aspect of this game; it is easy and provides you with a little bit of respite between the reading stages. The Pixel graphics lent the game a nostalgic feel, reminding me of playing on my colour Gameboy. Some people may find the low resolution a bit of an issue but all I can say is, do not worry about it. Great price point, only $2.99 for practically three games. No voice over in this game, however the soundtrack is good. Positives: ~~~~~~~ -	Three short and rich stories -	Interesting characters -	Nice Pixel graphics -	Achievements and trading cards Negatives: ~~~~~~~~ -	Combat phase could have been better LiEat series are well written and enjoyable to play (mostly reading).  Whether you already like this genre or have not yet been introduced to it, I recommend this series. 8/10 Key provided by developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

title: LiEat
text: There isn't an RPG I know of that has held such charm and innocence above it's rather darkly surreal world like LiEat. You play as Theobald Leonhearts and his dainty companion Efina through 3 games, each taking place after one another. You follow them through 3 different settings each one sprinkling you bite-sized bits of Theo's and Efi's personality and past while foreshading a deeper meaning to your adventures. Each game plays the same way only differing in story and setting so the game will be evaluated in a general sense. Soundtrack The sound design in the game works well but isn't anything special at all. It gets moody or bright when it needs to be. Overall the music seems to give off the feeling of bittersweetness which is fitting for the game. Gameplay The gameplay here is what you expect of an RPG with a little twist where you can decide if you indeed want to engage or not in combat beased on being given an option to decided whether or not a lie is genuine or not. This makes the combat pretty much optional save for the bosses and the few unavoidable fights. However the ending you recieve can be determined by your character level but unfortunetly the enemy scaling is really bad. All the enemies save for boss characters are lies in a physical creature-like form and it is possible to get strong enough to destroy the bosses by grinding on the weakest enemies. They just give you way to much exp and this becomes more apparent each game the first being the most balanced in my opinon. I also find it odd you get money too but never use it for anything. The game progresses for the most part by speaking with characters or checking objects in a sequential matter which is sometimes boring to be honest. Sometimes this leads you to pressing 'Z' on everything you come in contact with or searching around far too long. This also led to me finding the legendary weapons in both the 2nd and 3rd games which was pretty cool because they were hidden invisibly but they really break the game and I don't recommend even picking them up unless you just want to enjoy the story. In the second game you can find the legendary weapon on the second screen right at the beginning which is very unfortunate but the thrid game fixes this. Overall the gameplay is fine if a little imbalanced and sometimes mundane. It seems comfortable not taking the idea of deciding which lies are genuine further than a plot device rather than a real  fight mechanic. I liked that Efi follows you like Pikachu would in the old Pokemon games but was dissapointed that I couldn't turn around to converse with her. Story The story is the meat of this game in my opinion but it sure takes it's time selling you on it and I really felt like most of it was in the 3rd game while the other 2 were just primers for the big drop. It's not the best but not the worst and once I was learning more about Theo and Efi I definetly wanted more and the game delivers well on that part. This game contains interesting lore where dragons are born with human appearences and each with a special ability and it delves a bit into the idea but often I found that the abilities were pretty lame. For the most part the characters you engage with are interesting and have a personality that is acceptable but they are mostly forgettable. Sometimes the dialog makes no sense given the context an example of this is the responses you get from the maids after completing the investigation on them in the 3rd game. The most enjoyable moments here are the interactions between Efi and Theo. LiEat is an RPG mostly centered around it's story and the relationship between the two main characters. The combat is almost optional and could use some work to balance out. The settings could be better since the 2nd and 3rd game's are too similar. It is thematicly cute feeling but keeps a dark and surreal tone when it comes to the plot devices which was pretty neat. Overall it is enjoyable but rough around the edges at times. You can tell if this game is going to be enjoyable for you almost immediatly. I say follow your gut on whether or not you want to play this one because it is an experience that is varied but what is appealing about it very apparent and doesn't stray far from that.  Graphics The art design is what you would expect from an RPG Maker game however LiEat sets itself apart from the others with it's brief animations which are usually used to introduce a character for the first time or during key events. The static images that are sometimes used instead of an animation in these sequences are okay, they usually feature a character posing cooly. My only gripe here is the character portraits that appear when one of them is talking. They are cool looking but are harsh on the eyes to make out the smaller details in them. For me this was a 6/10 slightly above average but could have been a 7 if the game had a little more strategy involved in the combat it was just too much of a breeze. I enjoyed it in parts but didn't in others but I'd still recommend becasue the price is very fair for what it offers.

title: Lili: Child of Geos - Complete Edition
text: Lili: Child of Geos is one of the bizarrest games I ever played: an open-world flower picking simulator with a stroke of the RPG-brush. You play Lili, who visits an inhabited island to collect flowers for a school project. But she does not pick these flowers from the fields or gardens, she only picks the ones that grow along the streets and on the monsters. Yes, this game features flower-picking based fighting. You chase a monster and then, during the actual fight, you pluck flowers off the monster. Maybe using the mouse makes it too easy, but I never lost one of these fights. To be fair, this fighting model makes more sense on a touchscreen device. This is not as surprising since earlier editions of Lili: Child of Geos were published for mobile devices. And after all, it seems new and creative to me. But the open world of Lili: Child of Geos offers a bit more than flower picking. You can explore, collect stuff, talk to people and solve sidequests which consist of exploring, collecting stuff and talking to people. Lili: Child of Geos is rather short and small. It took me about three or four hours to do the main quests, all the side quests and get all the nonrespawning collectibles. On a more negative side, this game features no voice acting, only textboxes. So, was Lili: Child of Geos any fun for me? Yes, but not 20€ worth of fun, more like 10€. Conclusion: If you need a tiny charming open-world game for inbetween with an uhmm innovative fighting mechanic and this game is on sale, then give it a try.

title: Lili: Child of Geos - Complete Edition
text: I have mixed feelings about this game.  I thought I was getting a full "Zelda"-like game with a female protagonist and a unique combat mechanism, but this was just "Flower-Picking: The Game," with occasional optional fetch quests. I'm not even sure what demographic this was meant for; the dialogues, humor, and videogame references are older-teenager appropriate, whereas the gameplay is simplified enough for an elementary student to master.  Likewise, The main character looks like she's 15 and acts like she's 12, but is supposed to be a graduate student, and has apparently played every old school videogame on the planet except for Zero Wing... even the other characters in the game couldn't place her age. What I liked about this game: - The visuals and character designs were interesting, creative, and well-crafted.  I really enjoyed the overall look and atmosphere of the game, and the attention to detail of the artists. - The game's frequent references to other videogames and movies, the dark humor, and the sassy side comments.  It was worth it to keep talking to characters and to read all the Mayor's signs. - The balanced learning curve. - The ability to pick up wearable items like ridiculous masks, videogame hats, and flying pets. What was okay: - The core game mechanic of picking flowers off spirits' backs.  While there was an increase in difficulty as the game went on (the introduction of thorns and bombs, the movement patterns of the spirit, the need to score higher combos of non-thorn flowers), there was not enough variation for it to feel appreciably different after about the 8th enemy.  The only real distinguishing factor from that point on was how long of a combo you needed in order to win 3 stars; early enemies only need 8-12 flowers in a row, whereas the final boss takes a chain of 30-40 flowers.  As you can imagine, by the 52nd spirit this minigame had worn out its welcome. - Sometimes you will be able to complete optional side quests instead of fighting, which fall into one of four categories: "find all the hidden things," "visit that place you just visited," "fetch an item from the chest you just opened," or "fight that spirit you just fought"... O.o - Four Hand Monty's "if you are short on cash and don't want to break vases" bonus ball-and-cup minigame. - The oversimplified inventory system that consists of three tiers of armor for each of your three stats, three one-use items that I rarely ever used, two kinds of currency, two levels of keys, a cheater's map, and a bottle that summons butterflies for no reason.  That's it, unless you count the treasure trophies that only exist for flavour. What I didn't like: - Being constantly interrupted by either Mailbox, or the Mayor, or the fish, with long blocks of dialogue that you can't really skip.  I'm all about witty banter and story progression, but considering you need to play through the game twice to get all the achievements, it would have been nice to be able to bypass the excessive chatter. - The big mid-game "choice."  I played through the game a third time, just to see what would happen if I chose the alternate path, and it was totally not worth it.  I was expecting at least a cutscene with the Professor. - The rainbow bird poo.  Seriously?  That needed to be a thing? - The achievements.  Some of them made sense, like the ones for beating the spirits, but some of them were needlessly tedious such as the "break 1000 vases" or "scare 500 birds." Additionally, these achievements are not cumulative across multiple playthroughs, you must break all 1000 vases using the same save file. There is also one broken achievement for this game: "unlock all doors."  It seems there was a discrepancy between the PC version and other ports, with the PC release only having 22/28 unlockable doors programmed in.  Thus, the achievement cannot be unlocked without manually altering the game code (you can find instructions for this online, but I personally didn't want to risk irreparably damaging my game data just for 100% completion).  [Edit 12/19/14: The broken achievement has been removed from Steam, so you can now get 100% completion!] Overall, I would give this game a 7/10.  I liked the setting and the humor, but the core gameplay and the achievements were tiresome and boring by the end.

title: Lili: Child of Geos - Complete Edition
text: If you are looking for a casual game that has a unique combat system, this is a good game to get. First off some of the most notable bad features: 1. The controls starting off suck. If you are using a controller. The game does not tell you what buttons do what. All the key maps are for the keyboard. That is until you start playing and enter combat. Then they show up as the controller keys. 2. The resolution cannot be adjusted in the game. You will need to edit the config file if you are not happy with the settings. (FYI that file is filled with junk you will need to sort through). 3. The storyline starts off very pathetic and Lili just decided to do whatever everyone wants, With those out of the way, you have a short, lighthearted adventure game. You play Lili who ends up on the island looking for flowers for her Vegi-magic college assignment. There are 3 types of inhabitants on the island. The constructs are the ones you will interact with for quests. The fish will give you general information and the spirits are the guys you need to battle to get the special flowers. The story starts off slow and progresses more about Lili's life and the freedom of the constructs. The enphasis on flowers starts to slowly go away as the quest to defeat the evil mayor takes full stage. The combat system in this game is a bit different. Both good and annoying. You must jump on the back of the spirit and collect flowers. Once you jump on them, thorns, flowers, and bombs pop up on their backs. It is your job to hit the right button coresponding to the flowers and bombs. Get enough flowers in the timeframe and you defeat it. Fail and you just fall off and have to run back up to it and try again. There is no dying in this game so you can keep trying all you want. The graphics are beautifully done. The locations are vivd with life. For the most part, all with the exception of a few constructs look uniquely different. The spirits look almost exactly the same but with different masks. Each location although foresty has its individual look and feel. Definitely a good looking game. I played it on my 4K tv and the resolution defaulted to that. (When you first log in the game sets the resolution to your systems max even if you do not want it to.) The game is definitely not hard to beat and ranges from 4 to 9 hours to play depending on how many achievements you want. One thing to note is the abundance of game references and items from other games throughout the island. The dialong is quirky and not meant to be taken seriously. If you want a simple game that does require a little bit of action, this is a good game to get.

text: Do you love finding every chest, opening every lock, and breaking every vase in a game, the more the better? Try Lili, then--it's chock full of all of those! I find Lili a relaxing break: gentle music, lush scenery, and really, really strange characters and dialogue. I have trouble turning off the game, not because I want to beat one more monster, but because I want to talk to one more character to see whether there's another weird things to hear. title: Lili: Child of Geos - Complete Edition
text: Lili: Child of Geos is a beautiful and relaxing action adventure. When I saw screens of it I first thought this is probably some kind of highly polished hidden object game. What “sold” me was when I discovered you can actually walk this marvellous world. Item hint: + Beautiful somehow cuddly graphics + Mostly relaxing atmosphere + Okay story, hints to a possible prequel + References + Moderate length + Game advises to visit the options menu and asks to automatically determine graphics settings + Basically no grinding + Good controls 0 Unfortunately no voice acting 0 Different camera modes - Some advertising for another BitMonster game - Level cap, making it impossible to max out all skills with the same avatar - Flowers sometimes in places that are simply unreachable I started playing this game in the hope it would provide a counterpoint to Dead Island which had become exhausting and bullseye. After playing like 15 minutes I felt pretty relaxed. The game still has tense moments but all in all it's a pretty tranquil experience. Although the game's world is not too big it has an expansive feel to it, maybe because it looks lived-in or alive. The back story is rather light, maybe owed to the mobile origins of the game. You control Lili who has come to Geos as a Vegi-Magical student from the Gildern Magis College (with a deadline) but is quickly entangled in in the conflicts of a two-class society. Most NPCs have some depth to them which you learn by interacting with them, i.e. fighting the bad ones (Spirits) and talking to the good ones (Constructs). There is usually a reward for exhausting interaction. There are some indicators to a story that happened before so there may be a prequel. The Constructs are wood-based being making a disturbingly wood-based living in wooden houses with wooden furniture and wooden toilets, even toilet paper . There are a number of pop-references in the game and there is a mock pop-quiz where Lili can show off here extensive knowledge of games. There is also occasional, not too much, advertisement for another game by BitMonster. The game is of moderate length and may take you two evenings to complete. You can explore the world some more after you beat it. There are a number of achievements that may make you play some more and the “max out skill” achievements actually require you to stature at least one additional game – it took me not quite an hour to max out a single stat. Besides that there is almost no grinding. Unfortunately, there is no voice-acting. Instead there are a few generic sounds or words, e.g. “Hello”, and Lili's feelings are well-done by stances and facial expressions. With so many games not actually having any actual options, I found it interesting that the game starts out with advising you to go to the options menu and offers to automatically determine your machine's graphic settings. The controls work fine with the world's topology and are pretty tight with few exceptions. When chasing a Spirit it happened at times that instead of jumping onto them I suddenly found myself in conversation with a Construct or picking a flower because the game decided that was more likely what I wanted. Then you're supposed to collect flowers set around the world but a few of them are simply set in places Lili can never reach, e.g under bridges. There is a number of different camera modes that aren't listed in the games help - I didn't find any use for them. Activated them with keys Insert, Delete, Home, End, PageUp, PageDown, then move around a bit to see their effect. Lili: Child of Geos was a lot of fun and I recommend it. I bought the game as part of a bundle and probably wouldn't buy it for the full price (currently 10 Euros) but wait for 50% off. I'd be delighted  to see another game of this kidney, maybe a sequel or Orchid prequel.

title: Lili: Child of Geos - Complete Edition
text: This is an odd little game! Lili - Child of Geos is an open world adventure with light RPG elements which seems mostly oriented to younger audience. You play part of Lili, quirky graduate who has landed on an island with intelligent humanoid trees and masked "spirit" creatures with the mission of picking up all the rare flowers for her graduation thesis. Problem is, the flowers grow only on spirit's back, so she has to chase them, jump on their back and pluck flowers while they run frantically away. But not to feel bad for the spirits, cause they're all kinda jerks to the tree people who are basically their slaves. It has definitely got my recommendation. Firstly I'll tell what's good about it, then what problems does it have and lastly a conclusion. Pluses: +Graphic. Hands down. They're not exagerating the marketing pitch, the graphic is very nice for such a small, tablet-ported title, nice particle and filter post-proc effects hold on even to AAA modern game standards, and framerate smoothness is commendable. I couldn't manage to lower it under 60FPS anywhere - on rare loading points, on great city panoramas, anywhere! The framerate stayed rock solid stable. +Characters. Tree-people are generally original, are interesting, have charm and personality, and are diverse. Just the way it should be in an imaginative adventure game. Lili is really quirky and charming heroine. A bit simplified characterisation and motivation, which again begs the conclusion this was intended for younger players, but one can see she was written with heart. +Interesting areas. Areas are full of collectibles, small side quests (which usually give cosmetic colectibles) and secrets. It's fun to explore them. Again though, although one can wander around nicely exploring, the areas aren't huge, and can be completely scanned fairly quickly. The game isn't 10s of hours long, more like 4-8h (at the time of writing I had 1.7h registerd and, as I understand other reviews, I'm somewhere around the half mark. On the other hand, the areas are diverse and look lovely all in all. +RPG elements. Although somewhat shallow (4 skill gagues with some 5 stages overall) skill acquiring is a nice touch. Other RPG staple, equippable items is just cosmetic, but is my hat collection is even this early vide and fun to collect. Could have been more deep and flashed out, but better to have it like that than not at all. +Gameplay. As said, exploring the world overall is fun, plucking "minigames" arecahotic when played with mouse, but not too hard with few skill adjustments and prizes are satisfactory. Overall it does it's job well enough, although, yet again is somewhat simple. Now the minuses: -INABILLITY TO CHANGE KEYBINDINGS! I'm a leftie, goshdarnit, and having no possible option to change movement keys to anything other than wasd bothers me alot (if this review were just for me, I'd put here two minuses, 'stead of one). Arrow keys are already used for camera movement (which I already do with the mouse), so they're in the code, I just need an option to change them with wasd, but none exists. Connected to that is -GUI. It seems shody ('seems', not 'is'). It gets the job done, but it's obvious this is a tablet port, the buttons are huge on FHD and some standard shortcuts and usability options don't exist here. Nothing game-breaking, but it could have been better. -Shortness. The game has potential, could have been something much greater, but in it's heart it's a tablet game with tablet shortness. People are reporting around 6h gameplay time. Shame. -+Odd quirks. I... kinda can't describe in detail, but at the moments I'm experiencing strange tonal dissonances in the game. I can't put my finger for whom the game speciffically is. If it's for younger and/or casual audience, then why are there lots of standard gaming touches about modern computer games, and their respectable memes. And rest of the game is depicted like fairytale like fantasy setting. It's not entirely clear how this setting is connected to our world. Lili goes to magical university so 9/10 times I think I'm in fantasysetting, then suddenly the tone shifts to strange and disturbing. Not that I mind, disturbing fairytale has become regular trope in itself (and e.g. I love AM's Alice MR) but it kinda clashes awkwardly. The game doesn't want to commit fully to weirdness, but sprinkles it around in odd bits. It's not a problem, but sticks like a scrapwe on your keyboard you know you'll get used to eventually, but which distracts first 10 times you feel it... -Prize. For such a short game 20€ is a bit much. I bought it within a bundle, so it's definitely worth it, but full prize is a bit too much. Just a bit, but still. Conclusion: Interesting short casual experience with awesome graphic, great exploration and fun story. The game's not a masterpiece, but it doesn't try to be one. I recommend it without a doubt, IF it's on a discount.

text: At its core, the gameplay style of Lili: Child of Geos is a tablet game.  You pluck flowers off your target and the difficulty increases by increasing the required number of flowers needed to be picked and the introduction of dangerous objects that mix in with the object.  If my monitor had touch screen capabilities, I would be playing the game with my fingers.  Despite this simplicity the game is fairly enjoyable because it comes in combination with a fairly enjoyable setting and atmosphere.  If I were to compare it, it would have to be with the atmosphere of the first city you wonder through in JRPG games like Final Fantasy IX and Kingdom Hearts.  It has a joyous, adventerous feel that warms your heart.  Maybe not at full price, but I would certainly recommend this game if you want to play around in a happy setting with surprisingly well polished graphics and lighting.  I feel like this game is worthy enough for the developers to turn this into a series starring Lili in more adventures but with more RPG elements, more puzzle elements, and a larger world.

title: Little Inferno
text: Wow, this game is horrible. World of Goo was incredible, so i decided to try some more by the same guy, but this was just a waste of money. It's got good reviews... idk, maybe there was some artsy element that I missed, but I was just but I was just bored. So you start off with a tiny stash of cash and a small collection of toys you can order. You order stuff and it appears after a delay, and then you toss it in the fireplace and burn it, which always gives you a few more coins than you spent. Symbolism for the insatiability hunger of human consumerism maybe? Idk, but it got old in a hurry. Most of the toys react in some novel way as you burn them... the dragon breaths fire, the ear of corn has popcorn pop off of it, the moon changes gravity so things orbit it. I imagine you could make some tiny rube-golberg machines if you were so inclined, but the space is so limited that it's pretty limited so I didn't have much success. Also there are hidden combos of items. If you burn certain items together, you've completed the combo. Once you've got enough, you unlock new toys to burn. So a big part of the game is looking at the titles of combos and trying to guess which toys are required, which is easy when you've only got access to a dozen items, but once it's closer to 100 it starts to take some trial and error. A message about sitting in the same place, looking at the same thing, and still searching for novelty? Might be a meta commentary about spending too much time on a computer looking for interesting games, but that might be something I'm superimposing on the subject. There's a thin plot about a relation with the girl next door. You get letters, and exchange toys with her. She's fascinated by a mystery of the inferno. And the environment of the game, the whispers of the world outside the inferno are quite haunting. But, that was the only interesting part of the game that I could see, but there wasn't much of it. Anyway, eventually you hit on a mystic combination of items and burn the house down, and then you've got to find something else to do. The end. I usually enjoy artsy games and games with social commentary. World of Goo kept surprising me with understanded but poignant imagery. Little inferno though? No so much. I unlocked all the items and completed the endgame, in about 3 hour, which was much shorter than I like to see a $10 game take. Maybe there was symbolism I missed, but this was just a waste of time and money as far as I could see.

title: Long Live The Queen
text: I picked up LLTQ for $2.50 or $5 during a sale and am essentially done with it after about 5 hours’ worth of play. It’s surprisingly enjoyable but I can’t recommend it because it’s too short and weighed down by an overly complex skill system that will only appeal to a very niche market. First of all, I give it extra points for the amount of effort that went into all the different story options & skill choices. Critics say it’s too linear but that’s not entirely true. Having the same events occur at the same point in the story allows you to strategically plan how to overcome challenges. If random events were procedurally generated each time you played, you would only be able to survive by dumb luck. Also, you can unlock extra dialogue choices, outfits and hidden events depending on which skills you develop and actions you take. It is fun to fail at a skill check, possibly die, then replay and build your character differently and overcome a story obstacle. However, the further into the story an event occurs, the further you need to backwards plan for it. This gets complicated due to the labyrinthine way the story events snake together with learning skills & plotting mood adjustments (different moods give bonuses & penalties to learning different skills) and the only way to get around it is to write down some notes about which events occur at which times. While I appreciate all of the multiple endings and achievements available, unlocking those would require way more effort than most people would be willing to spend. The game does give you an option to export a text log of story events, but it doesn’t include any information about skill checks so it’s not nearly as useful as it could be. I was still having a pretty good time despite the flaws because I liked the story, but just when I felt like things were getting interesting, it ended. You only need to survive through 40 turns or so to win, and those turns go by blazingly fast when you already know which choices you’re going to make. LLTQ gets an A for effort but I simply can’t advise anyone to buy it unless the thought of manually charting out every story event, skill point expenditure & mood adjustment through trial & error appeals to you. It will keep you amused for a few hours and you’ll have no need to ever go back to it.

title: Long Live The Queen
text: Fantastic game with cute graphic, yet much more serious story. You are playing as Elodie and your job is to plan her day, so that she learn different things (crucial stat raising aspect), which is also linked to Elodie's mood (depending on it you may get boost for learning particular skill or the opposite, it may become harder). You also make important decisions. There are a lot of moments when your statistics gets verified and very often there is more than just one way of handling the situation (and failing to do so may even result in your death). This game is addictive and challenging, there are plenty of "easy-to-fail" moments, though it also deliver a lot of different endings. It has high replay value especially if you're aiming to get all of achievements. The only con is game's length - it my opinion it should take a little longer to raise statistics and game should take place during more than just one year of ruling. But this actually prove of how good this game is - I wish I could play it longer, with more options and more story. I recommend it :)

title: Long Live The Queen
text: This, was quite an interesting, unique and fun game! So, you control the princess, send her to classes to learn skills and get better at things, and do your best to avoid getting taken over or killed.  This is actually QUITE difficult, as there are many different ways for you to die, and you will experience quite a lot of them (but that's good, there's 3 achievements related to this).  So don't feel bad, or a failure, or anything: it's to be expected! The game shows you the 'checks' that it does to trigger certain events, so you can figure out something to try to do differently the next time around.  And this is certainly not a 'single playthrough' type game by any means: there are so many events that can trigger, and so many ways to try to do things, that you really can't help but try again and again to do something different!  (I put in nearly 30 hours just trying different things out!) The story is interesting, the characters have their own interesting personalities (and own different stories and actions that you figure out through multiple playthroughs), and the game is definitely worth it, even not on sale!  My only regret was that I got this game, promptly put it on my backlog of games to play, and only got to it now! PS: Since everyone else has already spoiled it... Avoid the chocolates.  If you can!

title: Long Live The Queen
text: A bait-and-switch of regal proportions, Long Live The Queen wears the facade of an anime visual novel about a young princess becoming a queen (and indeed still is that), but is at heart a complex stat allocation and time management game.  Every in-game week the princess can choose to study a wide range of seemingly mundane skills, but in the dramatic life of royalty any skill might suddenly become relevant, from World History to Interior Decorating to Archery, and the princess’s untimely death might lurk behind any unassuming door!  This leads to complex strategic trial-and-error gameplay in determining which skills are needed when, what actions cause which ripple effects, and how much slack is permitted while avoiding a point of no return.  The game itself is incredibly open-ended and allows for hundreds of winning skill combinations, all while still following a coherent and interconnected story, so as long as the player can keep the princess alive they can turn her into any kind of princess they want, even a heartless dictator, and watch as events unfold.  While the marriage of two rather polarizing game styles will likely alienate many prospective players, it is that same absurd combination which makes the game so unique and enchanting.
